blocks.text: The planet of those who never ended was beautiful at first sight, and that beauty was already a warning. The clone saw it from above like a polished stone, with still seas and continents of a green that was far too even, with no scars of fire or of winter. Below, the cities had no cemeteries. Nor did they have clocks. The people (similar to humans, enough to hurt) walked with the slowness of those who don't have to arrive anywhere. Their faces were neither young nor old: they were of an impeccable middle term, like a face that had forgotten the way to either extreme.

blocks.text: Andrés received that letter sitting in the courtyard, glancing sideways at Vicente's house, which was still shut, its windowsill empty. The coincidence struck him, once again, as a personal letter.

blocks.text: Those who never ended received him with courtesy, which is what a civilisation has left when it has time to spare. They showed him gardens, libraries where every book had already been read, a lake where nobody drowned because for centuries nobody had dared risk not knowing how to swim. A man, or a woman (the middle term had softened that too), said to him, in an unhurried voice:
blocks.html: Those who never ended received him with courtesy, which is what a civilisation has left when it has time to spare. They showed him gardens, libraries where every book had already been read, a lake where nobody drowned because for centuries nobody had dared risk not knowing how to swim. A man, or a woman (the middle term had softened that too), said to him, in an unhurried voice:

blocks.text: “At first we wanted it. Not to fall ill. Not to die. Not to say goodbye. We achieved it. Then our ‘afterwards’ ran out. You, who come from a world where some people still come to an end, do you remember what it feels like to be in a real hurry?”

blocks.text: The clone didn't lie. He carried in his memory the hurry of the storm, of the escape, of the birth on the Moon, of Lía running across the courtyard on their return. He also carried the new unhurriedness of Andrés, the one on the shore, who no longer aged and sometimes, during afternoon naps, didn't know what to do with the hours.

blocks.text: “Hurry,” he said, “isn't only fear. It's that something matters now, and not later.”

blocks.text: The other nodded, with an envy so ancient it no longer burned: it only gave a faint light, like a lighthouse at noon.
blocks.html: The other nodded, with an envy so ancient it no longer burned: it only gave a faint light, like a lighthouse at noon.

blocks.text: “We've lost that. We preserve things. We don't wait for them. If you like, stay. Here you won't come to an end any more than you already don't. Here letters are superfluous, because there's nothing urgent to tell.”

blocks.text: Andrés, in Lo Pagán, closed his eyes. He felt, with a clarity that chilled him, the desert of an immortality without a shore: an even green, a safe lake, a face that never reaches either winter or summer. He had stayed in order to live without illness, beside Aya, beside the Mar Menor. That wasn't this planet. But it could come to resemble it, if he forgot the cup, the slow clock, the tomato that ripens or doesn't, the daughter who had chosen to come to an end.

blocks.text: “I'm not staying,” said the clone, and the man on the shore said it with him, without having agreed to, which is the strangest and most faithful way of being two. “I have a shore. He has a house. Even if we don't come to an end, there's still hurry there: the hurry to go back, to ask, not to correct what you don't understand.”

blocks.text: Before leaving, he asked to see, if there was such a place, somewhere these beings remembered those who had come to an end before the great remedy. They took him to an empty courtyard, with a single tree and a nameless stone. There were no dates. Someone, long ago, had polished them away, because dates offend those who never end. The clone left there, as he had left salt in the twilight, a pinch of earth from Lo Pagán that he still carried in a seam. Earth with time inside it.

blocks.text: When the letter closed, Andrés got up and went to Vicente's door. He didn't go in. He laid his hand on the wood, which did grow old, and spoke to the man who was no longer there, because in Lo Pagán people speak to the absent without asking doctrine for permission.

blocks.text: “You came to an end,” he said. “I don't. It's not that I got it right. It's that I asked for something else. Your house is still a house. And a life, too, even if it ends.”

blocks.text: Aya caught up with him in silence. She didn't ask whether the letter had been hard. She saw it in his back.

blocks.text: That same week, Madrid came again. Not Helena, this time, or not only her: a small board, one of those serene voices that in 2060 sold the correction of life. The priceless tomato had left Nexum without its old trade; now, with the bridge of the letters, someone had smelled a new product. “Correspondence between worlds. Live the faraway without leaving. A letter for every home.” They said it the way you describe a public service, and underneath you could hear the old appetite for patents, disguised as the common good.

blocks.text: Lía received them in the courtyard, standing, with Andrés and Aya behind her, and didn't let them quite sit down.
blocks.html: Lía received them in the courtyard, standing, with Andrés and Aya behind her, and didn't let them quite sit down.

blocks.text: “No,” she said, before the sentence was finished. “The bridge has no owner, and it doesn't get packaged. My father isn't a counter for universes. The one who searches isn't a petrol pump. If someone wants a sky, let them look at this one, at night, which belongs to everybody. If someone wants a world, let them live their own.”

blocks.text: The envoy, who was young and not entirely cynical, ventured an objection:
blocks.html: The envoy, who was young and not entirely cynical, ventured an objection:

blocks.text: “If knowledge of other worlds is shared, isn't that what you yourself did with the tomato? No owner, no price?”
blocks.html: “If knowledge of other worlds is shared, isn't that what you yourself did with the tomato? No owner, no price?”

blocks.text: Lía looked at him with patience, which is not condescension.
blocks.html: Lía looked at him with patience, which is not condescension.

blocks.text: “The tomato heals harm, if it's asked for. Someone else's life put into your mind isn't a fruit. It's an intimacy. I don't sell mine. He doesn't sell his. And I'm not going to open anyone's harbour so that a company can charge for the dizziness.”

blocks.text: Andrés added, with the same bluntness as when he had refused the patent on the Moon:
blocks.html: Andrés added, with the same bluntness as when he had refused the patent on the Moon:

blocks.text: “My daughter isn't sold in pieces. Nor am I. Nor is the one who left. He's seen a planet of people who never end and have grown bored of themselves. That's knowledge too. Take that one, if you like; it's free: not everything that can be given should be given.”

blocks.text: Aya, with the calm that came from Eva, asked:
blocks.html: Aya, with the calm that came from Eva, asked:

blocks.text: “Which is more dangerous: a letter with no owner, or an owner of all the letters?”
blocks.html: “Which is more dangerous: a letter with no owner, or an owner of all the letters?”

blocks.text: None of those who had come from Madrid gave a full answer. They left, the way people leave who haven't yet learned to lose. Helena, that night, called on her own, from her slow staircase, and said only:

blocks.text: “I didn't sign that. I'm glad you said no. Look after the bridge. Appetites, as you know, come back.”

blocks.text: In the chip, MAY left the questions on the table without clearing them away:
blocks.html: In the chip, MAY left the questions on the table without clearing them away:

blocks.text: *If everyone lived someone else's life, who would live their own? If an eternity is shared as a service, is it still a life, or is it a product you haven't yet given its proper name?*
blocks.html: If everyone lived someone else's life, who would live their own? If an eternity is shared as a service, is it still a life, or is it a product you haven't yet given its proper name?

blocks.text: Eva, closer:
blocks.html: Eva, closer:

blocks.text: *If a man doesn't come to an end, and his daughter does, whom is this house's time for? For the one who lasts, for the one who leaves, or for the while in which they coincide?*

blocks.text: Andrés, that night, didn't want a letter. He stayed on the doorstep with Aya and Lía, looking at the Mar Menor, which ended with every wave and came back, which is a different eternity, humbler, more of the shore. He thought of the single tree, of the stone without a date, of Vicente, of Helena climbing her stairs, of Iago, who would come to an end, of Lía, who would come to an end, of Aya and himself, who wouldn't.

blocks.text: “I don't want an even green,” he said at last. “I want this water, which sometimes gets dirty. And I want you, Lía, to keep the winter. Even though I don't have it. Even though it hurts me.”

blocks.text: Lía squeezed his hand.

blocks.text: “I'll keep it,” she said. “In return, don't let them polish away your dates. Yours, even if they don't end you, are still yours. And this shore's are too.”
